semantic_distinctions.meaning: The source treats ionic bonding in solids as a collective lattice interaction, not merely one isolated cation-anion pair.
Bonding is treated as a continuum; ionic compounds retain some covalent character.
Bond energy concerns mean gaseous bond breaking, while lattice energy concerns formation of the crystalline ionic solid from gaseous ions.
Crystal lattice energetics and solution-phase ionic/salt-bridge binding are different physical contexts.
Fajans-rule polarization of an anion electron cloud is explicitly distinguished from displacement of ions in a lattice by an applied electric field.
Ionic solids generally require a collective lattice description rather than discrete localized two-atom bonds.
Charge neutrality usually imposes stoichiometric ratios, but mixed ionic/metallic systems can exhibit non-stoichiometry.

nodes.label: Ionic bond
nodes.description: Chemical bonding involving electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; primary interaction in ionic compounds.

nodes.label: Electrostatic attraction
nodes.description: Attraction between oppositely charged electric charges.

nodes.label: Ion
nodes.description: Atom or group of atoms carrying net electrostatic charge.

nodes.label: Cation
nodes.description: Positively charged ion formed when an atom or group has fewer electrons than protons.

nodes.label: Anion
nodes.description: Negatively charged ion formed when an atom or group has more electrons than protons.

nodes.label: Electron
nodes.description: Negatively charged particle transferred or redistributed in ionic-bond formation.

nodes.label: Proton
nodes.description: Positively charged constituent of nuclei; contributes to net ionic charge.

nodes.label: Electrovalence
nodes.description: Electron transfer associated with ionic bonding, contrasted by the source with covalence.

nodes.label: Covalence
nodes.description: Electron sharing associated with covalent bonding.

nodes.label: Covalent bond
nodes.description: Bonding based on sharing electrons between atoms.

nodes.label: Metallic bond
nodes.description: Chemical bonding mode associated with metallic materials.

nodes.label: Ionic character
nodes.description: Degree to which bonding behavior is ionic rather than covalent.

nodes.label: Covalent character
nodes.description: Degree to which bonding involves shared electron density.

nodes.label: Polar covalent bond
nodes.description: Bond with partially ionic and partially covalent character.

nodes.label: Electronegativity
nodes.description: Tendency relevant to electron attraction; difference between bonded atoms correlates with ionic character.

nodes.label: Valence shell
nodes.description: Outer electron shell involved in common ionic-bond formation.

nodes.label: Valence electron
nodes.description: Electron in the outer shell that can be transferred in common ionic bonding.

nodes.label: Stable electronic configuration
nodes.description: Electron configuration sought through electron loss/gain; often noble-gas-like for s- and p-block elements.

nodes.label: Noble-gas configuration
nodes.description: Stable configuration commonly reached by s- and p-block atoms through electron transfer.

nodes.label: Electron affinity
nodes.description: Energetic tendency of an atom to accept an electron.

nodes.label: Ionization energy
nodes.description: Energy required to remove an electron; low values favor cation formation.

nodes.label: Redox reaction
nodes.description: Reaction involving oxidation/electron loss and reduction/electron gain.

nodes.label: Electron transfer
nodes.description: Transfer of electron density from donor atom/species to acceptor.

nodes.label: Lattice energy
nodes.description: Enthalpy change associated with forming a crystalline ionic solid from gaseous ions as defined in the source.

nodes.label: Cohesive force
nodes.description: Collective attraction holding an ionic crystal together.

nodes.label: Crystal lattice
nodes.description: Periodic arrangement of ions in an ionic solid.

nodes.label: Crystallographic lattice
nodes.description: Crystal structure arising from ordered ionic packing.

nodes.label: Stoichiometry
nodes.description: Charge-neutral composition constraint governing ionic-compound ratios.

nodes.label: Charge neutrality
nodes.description: Requirement that total positive and negative charge balance in a bulk ionic compound.

nodes.label: Ionic compound
nodes.description: Compound whose primary interaction is ionic and whose solid structure is generally a crystal lattice.

nodes.label: Salt
nodes.description: Ionic compound that can be formed by neutralization reactions such as acid-base neutralization.

nodes.label: Solvation
nodes.description: Process by which ions interact with and become stabilized by solvent.

nodes.label: Polar solvent
nodes.description: Solvent capable of stabilizing separated ions; water is the principal example in the source.

nodes.label: Aqueous solution
nodes.description: Water-based ionic solution containing mobile ions.

nodes.label: Molten ionic compound
nodes.description: Ionic compound above its melting point with mobile ions.

nodes.label: Electrical conductivity
nodes.description: Ability of a material or solution to carry electric current; ionic mobility enables conduction in molten/solution states.

nodes.label: Melting
nodes.description: Heating process that destroys the ordered ionic lattice and permits ion mobility.

nodes.label: Dissolution
nodes.description: Process in which an ionic crystal separates into solvated ions in a suitable solvent.

nodes.label: Acid-base neutralization

nodes.label: Arrhenius base

nodes.label: Coulomb's law
nodes.description: Electrostatic interaction law relating force/energy to charge and separation.

nodes.label: Interionic separation

nodes.label: Madelung constant

nodes.label: Born–Landé equation
nodes.description: Model for lattice energy using electrostatic potential plus short-range repulsion.

nodes.description: Thermochemical method for experimentally determining lattice energy.

nodes.label: Short-range repulsive potential

nodes.label: Electronic shielding

nodes.label: Fuoss equation

nodes.label: Equilibrium constant

nodes.label: Polarizability

claims.statement: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions or atoms with sharply different electronegativities and is the primary interaction in ionic compounds.
The source states that perfectly clean ionic bonding does not exist; ionic compounds retain some covalent/electron-sharing character.
Ionic compounds generally conduct when molten or dissolved, not when solid, and commonly have high melting points dependent on ionic charge.
Nearly full/empty valence shells, electronegativity, and electron-transfer tendencies drive common ionic-bond formation.
Ionic bonds are described as among the strongest bond types and ionic compounds are often stable.
Polar solvents can disrupt ionic lattices, solvate ions, and thereby produce conductive solutions.
Ionic bonding can arise from redox reactions in which low-ionization-energy atoms donate electrons and electron-affine atoms accept them.
Electrostatic attraction leads to alternating ions in a crystallographic lattice; discrete molecular units generally cannot be identified in the lattice.
Na and Cl transfer electrons to form Na+ and Cl−, which aggregate in a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio to form NaCl.
Charge neutrality imposes strict cation/anion ratios in ionic compounds, although some transition toward metallic bonding can yield non-stoichiometric compounds.
Salts can form through neutralization of Arrhenius acids and bases, exemplified by NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O.
Electron removal is endothermic, while electron acceptance and subsequent lattice attraction can release lattice energy and lower overall energy.
Ionic bonding occurs when the overall energy change is favorable; formation is generally exothermic but HgO is cited as an endothermic exception.

Charge magnitude strongly affects ionic-bond strength; a simplistic Coulomb-law comparison gives approximately fourfold stronger electrostatic interaction for 2+/2− versus 1+/1− charges when size/packing are ignored.
Ionic lattice structure depends principally on relative ionic charges and sizes; Pauling's rules help rationalize crystal structures.
Lattice energy can be determined experimentally with the Born–Haber cycle or predicted with the Born–Landé equation.
Born–Landé treats lattice energy as electrostatic potential plus short-range repulsion and uses the Madelung constant for crystal geometry.
The source gives −756 kJ/mol as a calculated NaCl lattice-energy value and −787 kJ/mol from a Born–Haber cycle.
In aqueous solution, Bjerrum/Fuoss relations describe binding strength as a function of ionic charges, while salt-bridge strength can be evaluated through equilibria.
Ionic bond strength can be modeled by Coulomb's law; cited ranges are approximately 170–1500 kJ/mol.
Small/highly charged positive ions can distort negative-ion electron clouds, creating charge density between nuclei and increasing covalent character.
Larger negative ions are easier to polarize; strong polarization is particularly associated with highly charged or very small cations.
Ionic bonding is dominated by attraction of ions whereas covalent bonding is based on electron sharing; ionic materials favor efficient packing rather than directional bond angles.
All ionic bonding contains some covalent character; greater electronegativity difference generally corresponds to greater ionic character.
Pauling estimated an electronegativity difference of 1.7 to correspond to about 50% ionic character on the Pauling scale.
Ionic character can be investigated through quadrupolar nuclei using NQR/NMR and nuclear quadrupole coupling constants.
In ionic solids the bonding is generally collective rather than a set of localized pairwise bonds; extended band/molecular-orbital descriptions can become appropriate.
As electronegativity differences decrease, materials can progress toward semiconductor, semimetal, or metallic-conductor behavior.
